prompt: What makes a value a secret, in the lesson's sense?

choices.text: It is long and random-looking
choices.why: Many secrets are, and a random-looking id is not a secret.

choices.text: Knowing it grants access
choices.why: Right. Whoever has it can act as the application.

choices.text: It is stored in a file called .env
choices.why: Where it is kept does not define it.

choices.text: It is encrypted at rest in the database, with a key kept elsewhere
choices.why: Encryption protects data; the key is the secret.

prompt: Which of these places hand a secret to everybody who will ever read them? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: the code in the repository
choices.why: Cloned onto every laptop.

choices.text: the repository's history
choices.why: Kept for as long as the repository exists.

choices.text: a log line shipped to a log service
choices.why: Read by several people.

choices.text: an environment variable of the running process
choices.why: That is how a secret should reach the process.

prompt: What do code, history, logs and screenshots have in common, according to the lesson?

choices.text: They are encrypted
choices.why: Not generally, and that would not help.

choices.text: They are deleted after a month
choices.why: Most are kept far longer.

choices.text: They are copied, kept and shared by design
choices.why: Right. A secret written there has been handed to every future reader.

choices.text: Only administrators can read them, and administrators are trusted
choices.why: Many people read them, contractors included.

prompt: When does detect-secrets-hook do the most good?

choices.text: Before the commit exists
choices.why: Right. Stopping a secret is far cheaper than cleaning one up.

choices.text: After the repository is published
choices.why: By then the secret has been handed out.

choices.text: Once a year, during an audit
choices.why: Eleven months of commits pass unchecked.

choices.text: Only on the production server
choices.why: The secret is in the repository long before.

prompt: How many potential secrets did detect-secrets-hook report in the first app.py?
The scanner reports a random-looking string in a test fixture that protects nothing. What is the right answer?

choices.text: Turn the scanner off for the project
choices.why: That loses every real finding too.

choices.text: Mark the line with the pragma, and say why
choices.why: Right. The reason sits on the line, where a reviewer can check it.

choices.text: Move the fixture into an environment variable
choices.why: It is not a secret; moving it adds nothing.

choices.text: Commit with --no-verify
choices.why: That skips every check at once.

prompt: A real key is stored in a variable called `x`, and the scanner says nothing. What does that show?

choices.text: The key must be safe
choices.why: Silence is not safety.

choices.text: The scanner is broken
choices.why: It works as designed: it reports what looks like a secret.

choices.text: A scanner reports what looks like a secret, not what is one
choices.why: Right. It is one defence; the rule of never writing secrets in code is the other.

choices.text: Short variable names are a security risk
choices.why: The name is not the risk; the key in the code is.

prompt: detect-secrets accepts a false positive marked with the inline comment `pragma: ___ secret`.
Why does `required()` raise instead of falling back to a default key?

choices.text: Flask needs an exception to start
choices.why: It starts fine without one.

choices.text: Defaults are slower to read
choices.why: Speed is not the issue.

choices.text: Python forbids default values in os.environ.get for secrets
choices.why: It allows them, which is the danger.

choices.text: A default would start production with a known key
choices.why: Right. Refusing turns a missing variable into an error somebody sees in minutes.

prompt: What does the `load` helper in test_app.py do before importing app.py?

choices.text: Clears both variables, then sets the ones the test asks for
choices.why: Right. Each test sees the module as it would start with that environment.

choices.text: Reads the .env file
choices.why: Tests never read the developer's .env.

choices.text: Starts the Flask server on port 5000
choices.why: No server is started.

choices.text: Deletes app.py from the cache for good, so that it is read again
choices.why: importlib.reload imports it afresh; nothing is deleted.

prompt: How does the lesson keep `.env` out of every commit?

choices.text: By encrypting it
choices.why: Not needed, and the key would then need a home too.

choices.text: A line in .gitignore
choices.why: Right. git check-ignore -v names the rule.

choices.text: By deleting it before each commit
choices.why: Then the application would not start.

choices.text: By naming it .env.secret
choices.why: A name hides nothing from git.

prompt: How many of the three tests failed against the first version of app.py?
A colleague writes `os.environ.get("PORTAL_SECRET_KEY", "dev")` so the app starts on every laptop. Every test passes. What is the risk?

choices.text: None, as long as production sets the variable
choices.why: The day it does not, nothing says so.

choices.text: A missing variable starts production with a public key
choices.why: Right. 'dev' is printed in the repository, and nothing fails.

choices.text: Laptops become slower
choices.why: No such effect.

choices.text: Flask rejects keys shorter than 32 characters
choices.why: It accepts them.

prompt: In a shell, `set ___` before sourcing `.env` exports every variable the file defines.
The key was removed from app.py and committed. Is it gone from the repository?

choices.text: Yes: git keeps only the latest version
choices.why: git keeps every version.

choices.text: No: the earlier commit still holds it
choices.why: Right. git log -S found it line for line.

choices.text: Yes, once the .gitignore is committed
choices.why: .gitignore affects untracked files, not history.

choices.text: Only on GitHub, not in local clones
choices.why: Every clone has the whole history.

prompt: Put the steps of rotating a leaked key in the order the lesson gives.
items: issue a new key at the provider
rewrite the history, if the team controls the repository

prompt: Why is rewriting history a second step, never the first?

choices.text: git filter-repo is slow
choices.why: Speed is not the reason.

choices.text: Rewriting history is illegal
choices.why: It is not.

choices.text: Copies made before it keep the old history
choices.why: Right. Clones, forks and CI logs are out of reach; rotation makes them open nothing.

choices.text: The provider must approve the rewrite
choices.why: The provider has no say over your repository.

prompt: Why deploy the new key before revoking the old one?

choices.text: Otherwise the reminders stop in between
choices.why: Right. Order avoids an outage of the feature using the key.

choices.text: Providers refuse to revoke a key with no replacement
choices.why: They revoke whenever asked.

choices.text: The old key becomes valid again if revoked first
choices.why: Revoked is revoked.

choices.text: git needs the new key to rewrite the history
choices.why: git knows nothing about the key.

prompt: The fix for a secret that was committed and pushed is called ___: a new key, and the old one revoked.
Match each thing a secret manager gives to why it matters.

pairs.right: the worker reads only the SMS key
a leaked copy expires by itself

prompt: What is the difference between an environment variable and a secret manager, in the lesson's words?

choices.text: Environment variables are more secure
choices.why: They are a channel, not a store.

choices.text: One is how a secret arrives; the other is where it is kept
choices.why: Right. The manager sets the variable the process reads.

choices.text: Secret managers replace the need for environment variables
choices.why: Most deliver through them.

choices.text: There is none: both are files on the server
choices.why: A manager is a service with access control and audit.

prompt: Why should the portal and the reminder worker not share one database password?

choices.text: Databases allow one password per connection
choices.why: They allow many accounts.

choices.text: Two components cannot read one variable
choices.why: They can.

choices.text: Revoking or leaking one then affects only one
choices.why: Right. One secret per purpose.

choices.text: Shared passwords expire faster
choices.why: Expiry is not shared-ness.

prompt: A screenshot pasted into a support ticket shows a configuration page with the SMS key visible. What is the first step?

choices.text: Delete the ticket
choices.why: Everybody who saw it, and every copy, keeps the key.

choices.text: Rotate the key
choices.why: Right. The copy in the ticket then opens nothing.

choices.text: Blur the screenshot
choices.why: The original was already seen and stored.

choices.text: Ask everybody on the ticket to forget it
choices.why: Not a control.

prompt: Which of these belong in `.gitignore` for this project? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: .env
choices.why: It holds the development secrets.

choices.text: __pycache__/
choices.why: Generated files, not source.

choices.text: app.py
choices.why: That is the source; it is meant to be committed.

choices.text: test_app.py
choices.why: Tests belong in the repository.

prompt: Which pair of defences from the lesson would have stopped the leak?

choices.text: Longer keys, and a private repository the staff alone can clone
choices.why: Length does not help, and private repositories are shared too.

choices.text: required() with a .env from the start, and a scan in the hook
choices.why: Right. Somewhere else to put it, and something looking before the commit.

choices.text: Rewriting history every week
choices.why: Cleaning up is not prevention.

choices.text: Encrypting app.py
choices.why: The key to decrypt it would need a home too.

prompt: Which tool does the lesson use to find when a string entered or left the history?

choices.text: git status
choices.why: That shows the working tree.

choices.text: detect-secrets-hook
choices.why: It scans files as they are now.

choices.text: git log -S
choices.why: Right. It finds commits that added or removed a string.

choices.text: git check-ignore -v
choices.why: It explains why a file is ignored.
